raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic systolic heart failure syndrome presenting toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause and typically with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <45% [1]. It occurs on the background of major gestational haemodynamic adaptation—expanded plasma volume, increased cardiac output and reduced systemic vascular resistance—which may unmask limited myocardial reserve [2]. Contemporary definitions emphasise PPCM as a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring careful separation from pre-existing cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, congenital heart disease, myocarditis, pulmonary embolism and hypertensive pulmonary oedema [3-6].

Incidence varies markedly by geography, ancestry and ascertainment. Systematic reviews and administrative studies show higher rates in women of African ancestry, in older mothers, and with multiparity, multiple gestation and hypertensive disorders [7-13]. In Haiti and parts of sub-Saharan Africa, PPCM has been reported far more frequently than in Europe or North America, although differences in referral pathways and diagnostic access complicate comparisons [14]. Preeclampsia is strongly associated with PPCM, supporting shared vascular and antiangiogenic mechanisms rather than a purely haemodynamic model [8].

Pathobiology is multifactorial. Early clinical studies identified inflammatory activation, cytokine excess and Fas-mediated apoptosis in subsets of patients [15-17]. A major mechanistic advance was the demonstration that oxidative stress can promote cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa fragment with antiangiogenic and proapoptotic effects on the microvasculature [18]. Parallel work implicated angiogenic imbalance, particularly excess soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 and impaired vascular endothelial growth factor signalling, linking PPCM to preeclampsia and multiple pregnancy [19]. Genetic susceptibility is also important: rare variants in dilated cardiomyopathy genes, especially truncating variants in TTN, occur in a meaningful minority and overlap with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy [20,21]. Thus PPCM is best viewed as a pregnancy-triggered cardiomyopathy arising from interacting vascular, hormonal, inflammatory and genetic vulnerabilities.

Symptoms are often nonspecific—dyspnoea, orthopnoea, cough, oedema, fatigue and palpitations—and may be misattributed to normal pregnancy or postpartum recovery. Red flags include resting tachycardia, hypoxaemia, pulmonary rales, elevated jugular venous pressure, new murmur, syncope or cardiogenic shock. Echocardiography is central, documenting reduced LVEF, ventricular size, right ventricular function, valvular regurgitation and intracardiac thrombus. Natriuretic peptides are useful because they are not substantially elevated in normal pregnancy, whereas troponin elevation may indicate more severe injury. Early versus late presentation can differ clinically, and delayed recognition is associated with more advanced heart failure [22].

Prognosis is heterogeneous. In the North American IPAC cohort, many women improved substantially, but severe baseline dysfunction, marked LV dilatation, Black ancestry and right ventricular dysfunction predicted lower likelihood of recovery [23]. Hypertensive disorders may define a partially distinct phenotype, sometimes with better recovery than non-hypertensive PPCM [24]. Recovery can occur beyond 6 months, supporting prolonged follow-up and avoidance of premature withdrawal of therapy in patients with residual dysfunction [25].

Management requires coordinated cardio-obstetric care. During pregnancy, treatment relies on diuretics for congestion, beta-blockers, hydralazine–nitrates when afterload reduction is needed, digoxin in selected patients, and anticoagulation when LVEF is severely reduced or thrombus is present. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are generally avoided before delivery but standard guideline-directed heart failure therapy should be introduced postpartum when compatible with breastfeeding and maternal status [29,30]. Delivery timing should be individualised: vaginal delivery is preferred when haemodynamically stable, while urgent delivery or mechanical circulatory support may be required for refractory shock.

Disease-specific prolactin blockade remains debated. A small proof-of-concept trial and a subsequent randomized multicentre study suggested that bromocriptine, added to heart failure therapy and accompanied by anticoagulation, may improve recovery in selected women [27,28]. Use varies by region and should balance potential benefit, thrombotic risk and the implications of lactation suppression.

Subsequent pregnancy is a major counselling issue. Women with persistent LV dysfunction face high risks of relapse, progressive heart failure and maternal death; pregnancy is generally discouraged. Even after apparent recovery, relapse can occur, so preconception assessment, shared decision-making and close surveillance are essential [26]. Long-term care should include repeat imaging, optimization of therapy, genetic counselling when familial disease or pathogenic variants are suspected, and attention to contraception, psychosocial health and cardiovascular risk reduction.
